title: Employer NICs threshold
headline: £5,000 a year since April 2025. Each £104 lower raises about £0.5bn.
description: Raise or lower the £5,000 a year (£96 a week) of each employee's pay on which employers pay no National Insurance, in steps of £104 a year (£2 a week), the unit HMRC publishes. Lowering it raises money from employers; the 2024 Budget cut it from £9,100.

baselinePolicy.text: Secondary threshold £5,000 a year (£96 a week) since April 2025, cut from £9,100 alongside the rise in the employer rate to 15%, and frozen until April 2031 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 47).
alreadyIncludes: Employer rate 15% and secondary threshold £5,000 from April 2025 (Autumn Budget 2024, Table 5.1 line 26).
Secondary threshold frozen at its current level until April 2031 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 47).

level.label: Employer National Insurance threshold (a year)
level.note: £96 a week, £5,000 a year; the slider moves in steps of £2 a week.

rows.label: Change employer threshold by £2 per week

uprating.head: nics
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR March 2026 forecast for this receipts head (ADR-0004).

caveats: HMRC publishes the effect of a £2 a week (£104 a year) change; larger changes are scaled linearly here, which HMRC warns is only approximate for thresholds. The range is kept to ten steps down for that reason.

HMRC's estimates are on its Spring Statement 2025 indexed baseline for an April 2026 start. This tool shifts the profile to the chosen start year and scales it by the growth of the relevant OBR receipts head in the March 2026 forecast; the underlying level is not rebased. HMRC deferred its 2026 edition to review key assumptions.

considerations.text: HMRC's figure is a direct effect on this tax and closely related tax bases. It includes HMRC's standard behavioural response (for personal taxes, through taxable income elasticities and tax-motivated incorporation), but not wider effects on the economy such as inflation or investment, which HMRC says are usually captured in the OBR's economy forecast instead.

The manifesto promised not to increase National Insurance. The government's reading, when it raised the employer rate and cut this threshold in October 2024, was that the promise covered the National Insurance working people pay; critics read it the other way. The desk does not treat an employer-side rise as a red line, and the argument would be had again.

HMRC postponed the 2026 edition of these estimates (due 7 July 2026) to complete a review of the key assumptions behind some of them, after the Office for Statistics Regulation asked for more transparency about pre- and post-behavioural estimates. The figures here are HMRC's June 2025 estimates.

interactions.text: The threshold and the employer rate work on the same payroll: a lower threshold brings more pay into charge, and a higher rate then applies to it, so the two together raise more than the sum of each alone.

indexation.note: Frozen in cash terms until April 2031 (Budget 2025).
